paragraph.text: D6. "It's cultural; criticizing it is ethnocentric"

respecting cultures doesn't mean accepting everything that happens in them. People who use this argument rarely apply it to every practice: almost no one would say child marriage or female genital mutilation are beyond criticism because they're traditional in some places. And cultures aren't fixed blocks: within each one there are people who question their own practices, as the debates over bullfighting in Spain, Colombia and Mexico show, and veganism mostly criticizes the speaker's own dominant culture, not other people's.
"You can't judge other cultures. This is part of our identity. That's cultural imperialism."
Different cultures have different values and practices.
Historically, criticizing other cultures often served to justify domination.
There's no neutral point of view from which to judge all cultures.
So criticizing cultural practices involving animals is ethnocentric.
P1 and P2 are true and important. Colonialism used "civilization" as an excuse. The problem is moving from there to the idea that no cultural practice can be criticized.
fails at P3, taken to the extreme, and in the conclusion, which would make it impossible to criticize any practice, including those the person arguing condemns.
"Criticizing meat-eating imposes Western values on other peoples."
"Rodeos, bullfights and circuses are culture." (which is I17)

Every place has its own festivals, foods and customs, and it's good to learn about them and respect them. But if a custom hurts someone, we can talk about it, even if it's a tradition. Many places have already changed customs that hurt people or animals, and they're still themselves.

Respecting a culture isn't accepting everything in it. People who say this usually criticize dogfighting or eating dogs in other countries, so they don't really believe no cultural practice can be judged. Cultures also change from within: Colombia passed a law in 2024 banning bullfighting from 2027, and Mexico City banned wounding or killing bulls in the ring in 2025. Practices that harm women and children, like child marriage and female genital mutilation, have been or still are cultural in some places, and they are recognized internationally as human rights violations. And veganism mainly criticizes the culture of whoever is speaking, which is the dominant culture, not that of some distant people.
"If a practice that harms women and children were cultural, would criticizing it be ethnocentric?"

If the argument held, it would hold for all of them. Since it isn't applied to all of them, the real criterion isn't "it's cultural" but "it's my culture".
Almost no one believes every cultural practice is beyond criticism. The argument tends to appear to protect the practices of whoever is arguing, not those of others.

text.bold: 2. Many societies have already changed their own traditions involving animals.

paragraph.text: In 1835 the United Kingdom banned cockfighting and the baiting of bulls and bears with dogs, and cockfighting is now banned in every US state. Bullfighting shows how this debate happens within cultures themselves. In 2010, the Parliament of Catalonia banned it; in 2016, Spain's Constitutional Court annulled the ban, holding that a region may regulate bullfighting but not ban it, and even so there were no more bullfights in Catalonia after 2011, at least up to 2020. Colombia passed a law in 2024 banning bullfighting from 2027, and in 2025 Mexico City banned the use of lances, banderillas and swords and the killing of the bull. Elsewhere bullfighting remains legal, as in most of Spain, in Portugal, in the regions of southern France with an unbroken tradition and in Peru, where the Constitutional Court upheld in 2020 the legal exemption for bullfights and cockfights. In Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court banned the
, in 1997, and cockfighting, for violating the constitutional ban on cruelty (D1). On both sides of these debates are people from the same culture.

text.bold: 3. Cultures also change where women and children are concerned.

paragraph.text: Child marriage and female genital mutilation have been or still are cultural practices in some places, and today they are recognized internationally as human rights violations. According to the WHO, more than 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone genital mutilation, practiced in about 30 countries in Africa, the Middle East and Asia; the organization notes that some religious leaders support abandoning the practice and that many health workers are becoming advocates for this among families and communities. According to UNICEF, child marriage has declined over the past decade but remains widespread: about one in five girls worldwide is married in childhood. Criticizing these practices isn't despising the peoples among whom they occur. As the political scientist Gerry Mackie showed, practices like these tend to end when families and communities themselves decide, together, to abandon them (D5).
Within every culture there are debates, disagreements and change. Many traditions around the world include vegetarianism, respect for animals or meat-free practices.
Vegans mainly criticize the dominant culture of their own country, to which they themselves belong. That isn't ethnocentrism; it's self-criticism.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: the problem is who criticizes and how

The most serious version says the problem isn't criticizing, but who criticizes and how: campaigns by rich countries against the practices of poor peoples or minorities reproduce colonial relationships, and veganism sometimes does this.

Concern about ethnocentrism is legitimate and important. History shows cultural criticism was often used to justify domination, and animal advocates should take care not to treat other cultures with contempt or pick easy targets among minorities.
But respecting cultures doesn't make everything that happens within them untouchable. The right question isn't whose practice it is, but who pays for it.
